sections.COMMENTS:
The Dinarides are a wide NW-SE fold-and-thrust belt stretching from southwestern Slovenia to Montenegro along the Adriatic coast of Croatia and inland. The Dinarides formed as a consequence of subduction and collision processes in the border zone between Europe and Adria tectonic plates. Adria acted, and is still acting, as an indenter moving roughly towards stable Europe and causing the Meso-Cenozoic carbonate rocks of the Dinaric platform to over-ride onto the Adriatic lithosphere (e.g. Aljinovic et al., 1990; Prelogovic et al., 1995; Herak, 1999). The most prominent structures of the Dinarides are NW-SE oriented thrust faults (Ivanovic et al., 1976; Mamuzic, 1975; Herak, 1991, 1999). Present day tectonic rates are mostly obtained from GPS campaigns and display general NNE-SSW to NE-SW trends, with values of 2-2.5 mm/yr in northern Dalmatia (Grenerczy et al., 2005) and 4-4.5 mm/yr in central and southern Dinarides (Grenerczy et al., 2005; Bennett et al., 2008; Devoti et al., 2008).
Within the Dinarides the seismicity is distributed along the entire length of the belt. Data on both instrumental and historical seismicity show earthquake activity across the entire width of the thrust belt. Available focal mechanism solutions (Herak et al., 1995; Vannucci et al., 2004) and structural geological data show, that at its NW end the seismic deformation is dominated by right-lateral movement on NW-SE strike-slip faults. In the central and southern part of the belt, both in the off-shore and coastal parts, thrusting is the prevailing mode of seismic deformation whereas in the inner parts of the belt the fault planes are steeper and show more complex kinematics with reverse, strike-slip and oblique movements. Active processes in this region are mainly driven by NE oriented compression, documented from maximum compressive axis orientation of focal mechanisms (Anderson and Jackson, 1987; Pondrelli et al., 2006) and from long-term geological evidence (Prelogovic et al., 2003).
This Source is a thrust fault running off Dugi Otok island reaching the mainland to the south of Split area, taking into consideration data on fault geometry and earthquake occurence (Kuk et al., 2000; Grandic et al., 2004). Geologic and earthquake data (Kuk et al., 2000; Grandic et al., 2007) give evidence of medium dipping reverse fault plane, belonging to a broader thrust/reverse fault zone emplacing carbonate rocks of the Dinaric platform onto the Adriatic platform and deforming internally.
In 1343 this area was struck by two earthquakes that reached a maximum intensity degree of VII-IX, one on 7 April and the other on 30 June (Shebalin et al., 1974; Albini, 2004), but no magnitude values exist for the mentioned earthquakes.
We set the average strike of the source in accordance to structural geologic data (Grandic et al., 2007). Average dip and rake of the source were set on the basis of structural data (Grandic et al., 2004) and seismotectonic characteristics (Kuk et al., 2000). We estimated the slip rate on the basis of horizontal velocities obtained by GPS campaigns (Caporali et al., 2009) and considering geometric characteristics of the fault.
